Materialism.summary: Consciousness is entirely physical. Every experience is produced by brains and bodies, and ultimately by the particles and fields of physics, with nothing nonphysical left over.
overview: Materialism holds that consciousness is a product of physical systems, chiefly biological brains, and that nothing nonphysical is involved. It is the working assumption of most neuroscientists, and their evidence is concrete. Damage part of the brain and part of experience disappears; stimulate it and experience changes. In the 2020 PhilPapers survey, 51.9 percent of professional philosophers accepted or leaned toward physicalism.

Most materialist theories aim to reduce mental states to physical ones, explaining a feeling by the brain processes that carry it. Reduction is optional, though. A theory qualifies as long as it admits nothing nonphysical. Some views identify experiences with brain states, some with functional roles, and some argue that experience as we picture it does not exist at all.

Its thirteen subcategories are Philosophical, Eliminative/Illusionism, Mind-Brain Identity, Neurobiological, Electromagnetic, Computational, Homeostatic, Embodied, Relational, First-Order, Higher-Order, Language and Phylogenetic. They run from U. T. Place and J. J. C. Smart’s claim that mental states are brain states, through Crick and Koch’s search for the neural correlates of consciousness and Baars and Dehaene’s Global Workspace Theory, to Paul and Patricia Churchland’s eliminativism and the illusionism of Daniel Dennett and Keith Frankish, which treats our sense of an inner felt quality as an introspective trick.

The central problem is what Joseph Levine called the explanatory gap. A complete account of which neurons fire, and why, still seems to leave open why that activity feels like anything from the inside, the puzzle David Chalmers named the hard problem. By Chalmers’s count, materialists answer in three ways. Some deny the gap exists, some accept a permanent gap in what we can know while denying any gap in what exists, and some expect future science to close it.

Philosophical.summary: Philosophical materialism holds that the mind is wholly a product of physical matter. Its theories set out the principles, definitions, and arguments that any materialist account of consciousness needs before the science begins.
overview: This group gathers the philosophers who frame the mind-body problem and defend materialism as a position. Materialism says everything that exists is physical, so thoughts, feelings, and experiences are entirely the result of physical processes. Today most writers call this physicalism. Its appeal is economy. Physics, chemistry, and biology have explained one natural phenomenon after another, and a materialist expects consciousness to follow.

The lineage is long. Democritus pictured a world of atoms moving in a void, and India's Cārvāka school held that consciousness arises from the four elements and perishes when they disperse. Thomas Hobbes described mind as motion in matter. John Locke grounded all knowledge in sensory experience, and David Hume dissolved the self into a bundle of perceptions. In the twentieth century the debate turned to how the mental relates to the physical. Functionalism defines a mental state by its causal role. Emergence treats consciousness as a higher-level feature of physical systems. Jaegwon Kim sharpened the idea of supervenience, under which no mental difference can occur without a physical difference.

Other entries defend the program against its critics. Owen Flanagan proposes a constructive naturalism, Alyssa Ney separates physicalism from scientism, and Daniel Stoljar argues that the puzzle of consciousness may reflect our ignorance of the physical world. Tim Bayne maps the structure of consciousness before asking about mechanism.

The open problem is the explanatory gap. Materialists can show that experience depends on the brain, yet no one has shown why any physical process should feel like something from the inside. Epiphenomenalism accepts a costly compromise. Experience is caused by physical processes but has no effect on behavior.

Eliminative.summary: Eliminativists and illusionists hold that the private, felt qualities of experience, often called qualia, are not real features of the world. The brain represents itself as having them, and that representation is what science must explain.
overview: This is the most radical position within Materialism. Most materialists accept that experience is real and try to locate it in the brain. Eliminativists and illusionists deny that there is any inner glow of qualia to locate. Science has discarded vital spirits and phlogiston before, and they expect phenomenal consciousness to go the same way.

Two strands run through the group. Eliminative materialism, defended by Paul and Patricia Churchland, holds that folk psychology, the everyday vocabulary of beliefs, desires, and sensations, is a flawed theory that neuroscience will replace. Saying ‘I feel pain’ uses outdated language for a set of neural processes. Gilbert Ryle prepared the ground by calling the Cartesian inner theater a category mistake, ‘the ghost in the machine’. Paul Feyerabend argued that mental concepts are revisable and could be dropped.

Illusionism is the milder strand. Daniel Dennett and Keith Frankish accept that experience happens, but say it is not what it seems. Introspection presents our states as having ineffable felt qualities, and that presentation is a trick of the brain's self-monitoring. Michael Graziano's attention schema theory supplies one mechanism. The brain builds a simplified model of its own attention, and that model describes attention as a mysterious inner awareness. Susan Blackmore and Nicholas Humphrey offer related accounts of consciousness as a model or a compelling user illusion.

The central objection is that an illusion of experience already looks like an experience. John Searle held that where consciousness is concerned, the appearance is the reality, so a convincing illusion of pain is pain. Frankish replies that the real task is the illusion problem, explaining why brains come to believe in qualia, which neuroscience can study directly.

Mind-Brain.summary: Mind-brain identity theory holds that every conscious experience is literally a brain process, one event described in two ways, just as lightning is an electrical discharge and water is H₂O.
overview: Identity theory is materialism in its plainest form. It claims more than that the brain causes the mind or that the two correlate. A sensation of pain and some neural process are one and the same event, reached by two routes, introspection on one side and neuroscience on the other. U.T. Place, Herbert Feigl, and J.J.C. Smart developed the view in the late 1950s, modeling it on scientific discoveries such as lightning being electrical discharge.

The founders separated meaning from reference. ‘Sensation’ and ‘brain process’ mean different things, as ‘morning star’ and ‘evening star’ do, yet each pair picks out a single thing. So the identity is a contingent discovery, open to empirical test. Smart handled vivid qualities, such as the green of an after-image, by treating experience reports as topic-neutral, saying only that something is going on like what happens when one sees green. Place called the belief in an inner screen of colored images the phenomenological fallacy. David Armstrong and David Lewis later combined identity with functionalism. Everyday psychology fixes the causal role of a mental state, and neuroscience finds the brain state that fills it.

Hilary Putnam's multiple realizability argument pushed the theory from the center in the 1960s. An octopus or a silicon-based creature might feel pain with a brain unlike ours, so pain cannot be one human neural type. Saul Kripke argued that a true identity between pain and C-fiber firing would have to be necessary, yet the two seem able to come apart. Joseph Levine named the explanatory gap. Even a true identity leaves unexplained why that process feels like anything.

The view survives in token-identity and restricted forms. David Papineau argues for identity from the causal closure of the physical world, and Brian McLaughlin defends a neurobiological version. The neuroscientific search for neural correlates of consciousness can be read as a hunt for identities.

Neurobiological.summary: Neurobiological theories hold that consciousness is produced by nervous tissue and nothing else. They try to pin down which neurons, circuits, rhythms, or brain regions generate it.
overview: These theories start from the brain as neuroscience knows it, with its neurons, synapses, circuits, and connectome pathways, and ask which of its mechanisms produce experience. John Searle's biological naturalism sets the frame. Consciousness is a higher-level biological feature caused by neuronal processes, as liquidity arises from the behavior of molecules. Ned Block's distinction between phenomenal and access consciousness supplies vocabulary that most later entries use.

The method came from Francis Crick and Christof Koch, who proposed setting metaphysics aside to search for the neural correlates of consciousness, the minimal neural activity sufficient for a specific percept. Most theories here offer a candidate. Bernard Baars's global workspace theory, given a neural form by Stanislas Dehaene and Jean-Pierre Changeux, says content becomes conscious when it is broadcast across the brain, with fronto-parietal ‘ignition’ marking the moment. Gerald Edelman grounded experience in selected groups of neurons bound by reentrant signaling. Jeff Hawkins treats the cortex as thousands of modeling columns that vote on a single percept.

Others move the search away from the cortex. Björn Merker argues that basic experience is generated in the upper brainstem, citing children born without a cortex. Lawrence Ward and Byoung-Kyong Min look to the thalamus, and dendritic integration theory places the switch inside single pyramidal neurons, whose apical dendrites decouple from the cell body under anesthesia. Georg Northoff shifts the question from place to timing, to the brain's spatiotemporal dynamics. A final pair draws out consequences. Robert Sapolsky concludes that a physical brain leaves no room for free will, and Kevin Mitchell defends real agency within the same physicalism.

The open problem is the step from correlation to explanation. Jeffrey Gray's account openly concedes that it explains the contents and function of experience without explaining why any of it should feel like anything. Finding the neurons that fire when a person sees red does not by itself show why that firing is felt.

Electromagnetic.summary: Electromagnetic field theories hold that consciousness is, or arises from, the electromagnetic field generated by the brain's combined neural currents, a single physical field that could bind scattered neural activity into one experience.
overview: Whenever neurons fire, their currents add up to an electromagnetic field that spans the brain. Most neuroscience treats this field as a by-product. Theories in this group give it a role in consciousness, either as experience itself or as the medium that produces it. The attraction is the binding problem. Color, shape, and sound are processed in separate places, yet we experience one unified scene, and a field integrates information across space at once.

Johnjoe McFadden's conscious electromagnetic information (cemi) theory is the strongest version and says the brain's field is consciousness. Susan Pockett identifies experience with particular spatial patterns in the field. Wolf Singer and Lucia Melloni stress large-scale synchrony, the gamma-band oscillations that briefly lock distributed neurons into a coherent ensemble. Rodolfo Llinás tied conscious states to oscillations in the brain. Earl Miller proposes that traveling brain waves perform analog computation, and that consciousness appears when those waves grow large enough to unify the cortex. Tam Hunt and Jonathan Schooler's general resonance theory builds on shared resonance and links it to panpsychism.

Evidence comes from several directions. Synchronized oscillations track conscious perception. Electric fields appear to carry working-memory content even as the specific neurons holding it change from trial to trial. Ephaptic coupling, in which a field influences nearby neurons without synapses, shows that fields can act back on firing, and weak applied fields entrain neural activity in brain tissue.

Critics ask for specifics. Showing that a field correlates with experience is easier than showing that it causes it, and the theories still lack a precise mapping from field patterns to particular experiences.

Computational.summary: Computational theories hold that consciousness is a kind of information processing. What counts is the computation a system performs and the roles its states play, so the right program could in principle be conscious in silicon as well as in neurons.
overview: Computationalism treats the mind as a computational system and mental processes as computations the brain carries out. It usually travels with functionalism, which defines a mental state by its job in the system, its inputs, outputs, and links to other states, and treats physical makeup as secondary. The appeal is that minds become open to the tools of computer science, and machine consciousness becomes a live, testable question.

Alan Turing set the stage with his imitation game and his model of a universal machine. Hilary Putnam proposed machine functionalism, comparing mental states to the states of a Turing machine. Marvin Minsky pictured the mind as a society of simple agents, none intelligent alone. Daniel Dennett's multiple drafts model replaces a single place where everything comes together with parallel streams of content competing for influence. Manuel and Lenore Blum built a formal conscious Turing machine on the global workspace model.

Other entries ground computation in brain dynamics. Stephen Grossberg's adaptive resonance theory says we become conscious of states in which incoming signals and learned expectations resonate. Terrence Sejnowski links computation to traveling waves across the cortex. The critical brain hypothesis holds that the brain runs near a phase transition between order and disorder. Nick Bostrom and Blaise Agüera y Arcas apply computational functionalism to whether simulations and AI systems could be conscious.

The standing objection is that computation is defined by abstract structure while experience seems tied to something more. John Searle's Chinese room argument describes a person who follows a program for answering in Chinese without understanding a word, and critics of computationalism apply the same reasoning to felt experience.

Homeostatic.summary: Homeostatic and affective theories hold that consciousness grows out of the brain's work of keeping the body alive and stable, and that feeling, the felt sense of how the organism is doing, is its most basic form.
overview: Theories in this group start from the body's needs. An organism must keep its temperature, energy, and chemistry within narrow bounds, and the brain regulates these internal states continuously. On this view, consciousness first appeared as feeling, the felt registration of whether things are going well or badly for the organism. Hunger, pain, and fear come first, and perception of the outside world is built on that base.

Antonio Damasio traces consciousness to homeostatic feelings built from the brain's maps of the body. Jaak Panksepp located primal emotional systems, such as seeking, rage, and fear, in ancient subcortical circuits shared by all mammals. Mark Solms argues that affect is the hidden spring of consciousness and places its source in the brainstem.

A second strand is predictive. Karl Friston's free-energy principle says living systems persist by minimizing surprise, predicting their sensory input and acting to make those predictions come true, a process called active inference. Anil Seth applies this to experience in his ‘beast machine’ theory, where perception is the brain's best guess about the world and the body, anchored in regulating the body's interior. Robin Carhart-Harris's entropic brain hypothesis links states such as psychedelic experience to the disorder of brain activity. Sigmund Freud appears here for his view that affect is irreducible and consciousness a surface over deeper processes.
The open problem is the step from regulation to feeling. Thermostats and single cells regulate themselves, so these theories must say what extra ingredient turns bodily control into something felt.

Embodied.summary: Embodied and enactive theories hold that consciousness belongs to a whole living body acting in its world. Experience is shaped by bodily form, movement, and interaction, and cannot be fully located in the brain alone.
overview: These theories reject the picture of the mind as a computer sealed inside the skull. For them the body and its surroundings are part of what consciousness is, as well as what it is for. A perceiver turns its head, reaches, and walks, and what it sees depends on those movements.

Two related ideas run through the group. Embodied cognition holds that thought is shaped by the body's physical form. George Lakoff and Mark Johnson argue that even abstract concepts rest on bodily experience, as when we speak of grasping an idea or of time moving forward. Enactivism goes further and treats cognition as action. Francisco Varela, Evan Thompson, and Eleanor Rosch introduced the term, and Thompson's later work ties mind to the self-organization of living things, making mind continuous with life.

Alva Noë argues that consciousness is something we do, an ongoing skilled engagement with the environment, which puts it partly out of our heads. Susan Hurley described the sensorimotor loops that link perception and action. James Gibson's ecological psychology holds that animals directly perceive affordances, the possibilities for action that the environment offers. Adam Frank, Marcelo Gleiser, and Thompson argue in ‘The Blind Spot’ that science overlooks the lived experience it depends on.

The group overlaps with phenomenology, especially neurophenomenology. Its main difficulty mirrors its appeal. Showing that the body shapes what we experience is easier than showing why bodily activity is felt at all. Dreams are a test case, since they are vivid while the sleeping body barely moves.

Relational.summary: Relational theories hold that consciousness is a relation, arising between subject and object, organism and environment, or brain and world, and so cannot be found in the brain's circuits taken by themselves.
overview: Most materialist theories look for consciousness inside the head. Relational theories look at connections. On their view, experience exists in an active link between a subject and something else, such as the object perceived, the surrounding environment, or another mind. This keeps the physical world in the picture as a working part of consciousness.

Andy Clark and David Chalmers's extended mind thesis argued that cognition can reach beyond the skull into notebooks, tools, and devices. Riccardo Manzotti goes further with his ‘spread mind’, identifying the experience of an apple with the apple itself as it takes effect relative to the perceiving body. Naïve realists such as William Fish and John Campbell hold that perception is a direct relation to ordinary objects, with no inner picture in between, and Campbell gives attention a central role.

Others treat the relation as structure. Douglas Hofstadter describes the self as a strange loop, a pattern in the brain that refers back to itself. Naotsugu Tsuchiya proposes characterizing each experience through its relations to other experiences. Kristjan Loorits applies structural realism to experience. Graham Harman's object-oriented ontology and William Jaworski's hylomorphism carry the theme into general metaphysics.

The difficulty is to say which relation counts. Brains, objects, and environments stand in countless relations that involve no experience, so each theory must specify what makes a particular relation a conscious one.

First-Order.summary: First-order theories hold that a mental state is conscious because of what it represents about the world. The felt character of an experience, such as seeing red, is the content of that representation, with no further awareness of the state required.
overview: First-order representationalism explains consciousness through world-directed mental states. When you see a ripe tomato, your visual state represents a red, round object in front of you. On this view, what it is like to have that experience is fixed by what it represents. The redness you notice belongs to the tomato, a surface property out in the world. The difference between seeing red and seeing green is a difference in the properties represented, and a pain differs from a tickle in the bodily disturbance each represents.

This answers an old puzzle. When you perceive orange, there is nothing orange in your brain. First-order theorists reply that a representation need not share its content's properties. The word ‘dolphins’ has eight letters, and dolphins have none. The transparency thesis adds that introspection finds no inner qualities besides the represented ones, since trying to attend to your experience lands you back on the scene.

Fred Dretske argued that a brain state becomes a conscious representation when it acquires, through natural selection, the function of carrying information. Michael Tye and Peter Carruthers developed representationalist accounts of phenomenal character. Frank Jackson, famous for the knowledge argument against physicalism, later adopted representationalism. On the neuroscience side, Victor Lamme's recurrent processing theory holds that feedback within sensory cortex suffices for experience, with no need for the brain-wide broadcast of global workspace theory. Ned Block argues that phenomenal consciousness overflows what we can access and report.

These theories define themselves against higher-order theories, which say a state becomes conscious only when the subject represents it. Their main problem is unconscious perception. Patients with blindsight respond to objects they say they cannot see, so first-order theorists must say what extra condition makes a representation conscious.

Higher-Order.summary: Higher-order theories hold that a mental state is conscious when the mind represents it, through a thought or inner perception about that state. Consciousness is a representation of a representation.
overview: Most mental states seem to come in conscious and unconscious forms. People respond to things they cannot report seeing, and they hold beliefs they never think about. Higher-order theorists ask what makes the difference and answer that conscious states are the ones we are aware of being in. A perception of red becomes conscious when a further mental state represents it. Without that second state the perception can still guide behavior, unfelt.

The theories differ on the nature of the higher-order state. David Armstrong and William Lycan described an inner sense, a monitoring system that scans our perceptions as the eyes scan the world. David Rosenthal's higher-order thought theory requires an actual thought, arising without inference, that one is in the state. Dispositional versions require only that the state be available to such thoughts. Uriah Kriegel's self-representational view puts the awareness inside the conscious state itself, so that each experience represents both its object and itself.

Higher-order theory has also gone into the lab. Hakwan Lau's perceptual reality monitoring theory treats consciousness as the brain's judgment that a perceptual signal is reliable, and notes that conscious perception and sensory metacognition both engage prefrontal and parietal cortex. Joseph LeDoux applies the approach to emotion, arguing that fear is felt only when it is represented at a higher level. Richard Brown, Axel Cleeremans, and Thomas Metzinger develop further variants.

Ned Block presses the central objection. A higher-order thought could misrepresent, describing a smell of vomit while the perception it targets is of crimson, and then it is unclear which experience the subject has. Animals and infants pose a second problem, since they may lack the capacity for thoughts about their own states.

Language.summary: Language theories examine how consciousness and language depend on each other. Few hold that language creates raw experience, but many argue that it shapes human self-awareness, inner speech, and the reflective consciousness that thinks about itself.
overview: This group gathers views on how consciousness and language relate. Language clearly fills human consciousness with content. The harder issues are whether experience needs language and whether language needs experience, and the answers depend on definitions. If consciousness means raw sensation, then requiring language would deny experience to dogs, preverbal infants, and nearly every other animal, and language appeared far later in evolution than consciousness. A loose enough idea of language, one that counts chemical signals between cells, allows language with no consciousness at all.

Most theorists conclude that basic phenomenal consciousness does not depend on language while its higher levels do. Self-awareness, reflection on one's own thoughts, and the sense of steering one's own actions lean on inner speech and grammar. Christof Koch argues outright that consciousness does not depend on language. Noam Chomsky and John Searle each examine how language and conscious thought connect, and W.V.O. Quine treated talk of phenomenal experience with suspicion from within his account of language.

The boldest claim here comes from Julian Jaynes. In his bicameral mind theory, people in early civilizations heard their own guiding thoughts as the voices of gods, and modern self-reflective consciousness arose only when that arrangement broke down, around three thousand years ago. Leslie Dewart ties self-presence to assertive speech. John Parrington links human consciousness to the joint evolution of language and tool use. Aaro Toomela treats language as the structure that organizes conscious human thought.

The open problem is the boundary. If basic experience needs no language, these theories describe a distinctively human layer of consciousness, and where words begin to change what experience is like remains disputed. Large language models sharpen the issue, since they produce fluent language with no settled answer about whether anything is experienced.

Phylogenetic.summary: Phylogenetic theories explain consciousness through evolution. They ask when and in which animals experience first appeared, what survival advantage it gave, and how simple sensing grew into the minds of mammals, birds, and octopuses.
overview: Most theories of consciousness assume evolution in the background. This group puts it in front. Following Theodosius Dobzhansky's maxim that nothing in biology makes sense except in the light of evolution, these theorists ask what process brought consciousness about and which creatures share it. Daniel Dennett, Joseph LeDoux, and Simona Ginsburg with Eva Jablonka all take this approach.

Most favor gradualism, with experience built up step by step from the simple stimulus and response of single cells. Ginsburg and Jablonka propose a marker, unlimited associative learning, the capacity to learn open-ended links between stimuli and actions, and use it to trace consciousness back to the Cambrian. Todd Feinberg and Jon Mallatt also argue for ancient origins, finding the neural basis for experience in early vertebrates and some invertebrates. Arthur Reber goes furthest and locates the roots of consciousness in single cells.

Comparison across species is the main tool. Peter Godfrey-Smith studies the octopus, whose large nervous system evolved separately from ours, as evidence that evolution built minds at least twice. Jonathan Birch develops ways to assess sentience across very different animals, and Kristin Andrews asks how much brain consciousness actually requires. Peter Halligan and David Oakley take a contrary line, treating experience as an epiphenomenon that benefits the species without directing behavior.

The hard question is survival value. Raymond Tallis asks what advantage a light-sensitive cell gains from being aware of the light, and finds none. If the first steps conferred no benefit, natural selection had nothing to work on, so an evolutionary story must explain why selection would favor felt experience over the same processing done unconsciously.

Non-Reductive.summary: Consciousness is wholly physical, a product of brains, yet mental properties form a distinct higher level that physical laws alone cannot fully explain. Minds emerge from matter and still do causal work of their own.
overview: Non-reductive physicalism tries to hold two positions at once. Everything that exists is physical, and the mind depends on the brain. Yet beliefs, desires and felt experiences cannot be rewritten as statements about neurons or molecules. The view grew out of problems with early identity theory. Hilary Putnam pointed out that the same mental state, such as pain, could be realized in very different physical systems. Donald Davidson’s anomalous monism held that mental events are physical events while denying strict laws that link mental and physical descriptions. Jerry Fodor argued that the special sciences cannot be reduced to physics.

Its main tool is emergence. At higher levels of organization, new properties appear that could not be read off, and perhaps never predicted from, the levels below. Many defenders add top-down causation, in which conscious states act back on the physical processes that give rise to them. George Ellis defends strong emergence of this kind, and Roger Sperry argued that consciousness steers brain activity from above.

The view also attracts religious thinkers. Nancey Murphy uses it to describe the human person without a separable soul, and Peter van Inwagen pairs a materialist account of persons with belief in the resurrection of the dead.

Jaegwon Kim pressed the strongest objection. If mental properties are irreducible, depend on physical ones, and also cause things, they compete with physical causes that already do the whole job. Kim concluded that the three commitments together leave the mind with no causal power. A further worry is how a property can be fully physical and still be impossible, in principle, to explain in physical terms.

Quantum.summary: Consciousness depends on quantum physics, or on other frontier physics such as extra dimensions, in a way that goes beyond the quantum behavior shared by all matter. Brains may exploit quantum effects, or mind and quantum reality may be linked at the root.
overview: Quantum theories hold that ordinary neuroscience leaves something out, and that the missing piece comes from fundamental physics. Two motives drive them. Quantum mechanics has its own unsolved puzzle about measurement, and consciousness is the other great unexplained fact, so some theorists suspect the two mysteries share one solution. Others argue more modestly that neurons, like the molecules of photosynthesis, use quantum effects to do something classical biology cannot.

The oldest version ties consciousness to the collapse of the wave function. Fritz London and Edmond Bauer argued in 1939 that the chain of measurement ends in an observer’s awareness, and Eugene Wigner pressed the point in 1961 with his ‘Wigner’s friend’ thought experiment. David Chalmers and Kelvin McQueen have revived the idea by pairing Integrated Information Theory with a physical model of collapse, in a form that quantum computers might one day test.

The best-known brain-based theory is Roger Penrose and Stuart Hameroff’s Orchestrated Objective Reduction, proposed in the mid-1990s, which locates conscious moments in gravity-related quantum state reductions inside neuronal microtubules. Others look to synapses (Friedrich Beck and John Eccles), nuclear spins (Matthew Fisher) or entangled spins at NMDA receptors. A third strand, including David Bohm’s implicate order, treats mind and matter as expressions of a deeper, holistic level of reality, and still others invoke hidden spatial dimensions or a universal zero-point field.

The standard objection is decoherence. The brain is warm, wet and noisy, and delicate quantum states should collapse long before they could influence neurons. Carlo Rovelli adds that an ‘observer’ in quantum physics can be a detector or a stone, so measurement gives consciousness no special job. Defenders of Orch OR point to recent reports of long-lived quantum effects in microtubules.

Integrated Info.summary: Information is a real, basic ingredient of the world, often more fundamental than matter, and consciousness arises from, or simply is, certain structures of information.
overview: Theories in this group treat information as something real in its own right. Computational theories under Materialism also talk about information, but there it only describes what physical systems do. Here it carries the weight. In many of these theories information is more basic than matter, energy or spacetime, and consciousness is what certain informational structures are, or what they produce.

The flagship is Integrated Information Theory, developed by the neuroscientist Giulio Tononi and later championed by Christof Koch. It starts from features of experience, such as being unified and specific, and asks what kind of physical system could have them. Its answer is a quantity, phi, that measures how much information a system’s whole carries over and above its parts. On this view consciousness is integrated information, and any system with enough of it, biological or not, has experience.

Other entries take different routes. David Chalmers’s double-aspect theory proposes that information has a physical side and an experiential side. Erik Hoel’s causal emergence argues that larger scales of a system can carry more causal information than its microscopic parts. Adam Safron’s Integrated World Modeling Theory combines integrated information with global workspace and predictive ideas, while Michael Levin and Paul Davies look to patterns of information that may lie beyond the physical altogether.

IIT draws enough criticism to have its own entry on the chart. Phi is practically impossible to compute for a real brain, and Scott Aaronson showed that the theory rates some simple, orderly networks as more conscious than people. Koch has also compared the theory with panpsychism, since it grants a little experience to a great many systems.

Panpsychism.summary: Consciousness is a basic feature of the physical world. The fundamental particles and fields of physics have experiential, or proto-experiential, properties, and in brains these combine into the full awareness of a human or animal.
overview: Panpsychism puts some trace of mind wherever there is matter, and perhaps wherever there is spacetime. Its appeal comes from the hard problem. If no arrangement of wholly nonconscious parts seems able to produce experience, perhaps the parts were never wholly nonconscious. The idea is ancient, with roots in animist religion, Greek thought, Leibniz’s monads and Indian schools such as Vedānta, and it has gained ground among analytic philosophers in recent decades.

The usual argument goes back to Bertrand Russell. Physics describes what matter does, its structure and dispositions, and says nothing about what matter intrinsically is. Panpsychists propose that this inner nature is experiential. Consciousness then needs no special origin. It was present all along and becomes rich and unified in brains.

Versions differ over where the mind sits. Micropsychism gives experience to the smallest physical units. Panprotopsychism gives them only proto-experiential properties that are not yet conscious. Cosmopsychism starts from the universe as a single conscious whole. Galen Strawson, Philip Goff and David Chalmers are leading contemporary defenders, and Alfred North Whitehead’s process philosophy treats moments of experience as the basic events of nature.

The hardest question is the combination problem. Nobody has shown how countless tiny subjects add up to one unified human mind, and Yujin Nagasawa argues the step may be impossible to demonstrate even if panpsychism is true. John Searle objected that consciousness comes in discrete units and cannot be spread over the universe ‘like a thin veneer of jam’.

Monism.summary: Reality is made of one basic kind of stuff that is neither mental nor physical. Mind and matter are two aspects, or two constructions, of that single neutral base.
overview: Neutral monism agrees with materialism and idealism that reality is built from one kind of stuff. It disagrees about what that stuff is. The base is neutral, and the mental and the physical are both organizations or aspects of it. This promises to avoid the interaction problem of dualism, the trouble materialism has with experience, and the trouble idealism has explaining how one cosmic mind divides into many.

The classic versions come from William James, who called the neutral stuff ‘pure experience’, and Bertrand Russell, whose ideas lie behind today’s Russellian monism. Ernst Mach built a similar picture out of sensations. Dual-aspect theories make the same move in another form. Spinoza described one substance known under the attributes of thought and extension, and the physicist Wolfgang Pauli, with Carl Jung, treated the mental and the physical as complementary aspects of one reality, an idea Harald Atmanspacher develops today.

The family is broad. It includes Max Velmans’s reflexive monism, Galen Strawson’s realistic monism, Max Tegmark’s proposal that consciousness is a state of matter defined by how it processes information, and the Qualia Research Institute’s attempt to give experience a precise mathematical formalism. Leibniz and Davidson are borderline members. Leibniz’s monads are mental and Davidson’s base is physical, yet each treats the mental and the physical as two coordinated descriptions of one order.

The weak point is the neutral base itself. Its defenders say little about what it is like in itself, and if it has experiential qualities, the view slides toward panpsychism, which differs mainly in calling the base mind-like from the start.

Dualism.summary: Consciousness requires something beyond the physical brain. A nonphysical mind or soul, distinct from matter, works together with the body, and in many versions it can survive the body’s death.
overview: Dualism splits reality into two kinds of thing, physical and nonphysical. In its classic form, substance dualism, the mind is a separate nonphysical entity, usually called a soul, that works with the brain without being part of it. It is the most widely held view of consciousness in the world, the default teaching of Judaism, Christianity and Islam, and it has deep roots in Plato and in Indian schools such as Sāṃkhya and Nyāya.

René Descartes gave it its modern shape. Mind is thinking, unextended substance, body is extended, unthinking substance, and the two meet in the brain, at the pineal gland in Descartes’s account. Interactionists such as Karl Popper and John Eccles, and more recently Richard Swinburne, hold that mind and brain act on each other in both directions. Epiphenomenalists let the brain cause experience but deny that experience causes anything in return.

Other versions soften the split. Property dualism keeps a single physical substance but gives it irreducible mental properties, and David Chalmers’s naturalistic dualism adds psychophysical laws linking the two. William Hasker’s emergent dualism has the brain generate a nonphysical self. A separate lineage running from Aristotle through Aquinas to Eleonore Stump and Edward Feser treats the soul as the form that organizes a living body, and it sits here because it refuses to reduce mind to matter.

Most professional philosophers reject dualism. The main charge is the interaction problem. If physics is causally closed, with every physical event fully caused by earlier physical events, it is hard to see how something nonphysical could move a neuron. Dualism also adds a second kind of stuff that Occam’s razor would cut, and it offers no clear method for learning how souls work.

Idealism.summary: Consciousness is the fundamental reality. Mind or awareness comes first, and the physical world, including brains, is derived from consciousness, exists within it, or is an illusion.
overview: Idealism turns materialism upside down. Materialists must explain how consciousness arises from matter. Idealists hold that matter arises from consciousness, or is a form consciousness takes, so the hard problem does not come up in its usual form. Each individual mind, human or animal, is a part or expression of a wider consciousness. The view anchors several religious traditions, especially those that began in India.

Its history runs on two tracks. The Upanishads identify Brahman, ultimate reality, with Atman, the self, and Śaṅkara’s Advaita Vedānta, Kashmir Shaivism and Buddhist Yogācāra developed mind-only views in detail. In the West, George Berkeley argued that to be is to be perceived, with God as the perceiver who keeps the world in existence when no one is looking. Kant, Fichte, Schelling and Hegel built German idealism, and F. H. Bradley’s absolute idealism carried it into Britain.

Idealism is gaining adherents today. Bernardo Kastrup’s analytic idealism treats individual minds as dissociated parts of one universal consciousness. Donald Hoffman argues that perception evolved to hide reality from us, and that the world is made of interacting conscious agents. David Chalmers distinguishes micro-idealism, grounded in the mentality of particles, macro-idealism, grounded in minds like ours, and cosmic idealism, grounded in a single cosmic mind.

Its central problem mirrors panpsychism’s. Panpsychists struggle to combine small minds into one. Idealists struggle to split one cosmic mind into many separate minds, and to explain why a world made of mind behaves with such lawful, shared regularity. Berkeley answered with God, Kastrup with dissociation, a mechanism borrowed from psychiatry.

Phenomenology.summary: Consciousness should first be described as it is lived, from the first-person point of view, before any theory of what causes it. The task is to map the structures every experience shares.
overview: Phenomenology studies experience as it shows up for the one having it. Edmund Husserl founded it around 1900 as a rigorous science of consciousness. His key method, the epoché, brackets the everyday assumption that the world exists independently of us. The point is to describe how things come to appear without first deciding what they are made of.

The method looks for invariant structures. Every experience is directed at something, the intentionality that Franz Brentano put at the center of the mind. Experience flows in time, each moment holding on to the one just past and anticipating the next. It is lived through a body, shared with others, and carries a quiet, pre-reflective awareness of itself, which Dan Zahavi calls ‘for-me-ness’.

Husserl’s successors took the method in new directions. Martin Heidegger replaced the isolated mind with being-in-the-world. Jean-Paul Sartre described consciousness as a ‘for-itself’ with no contents of its own. Maurice Merleau-Ponty placed subjectivity in the moving, perceiving body, anticipating today’s embodied cognitive science. Francisco Varela’s neurophenomenology and Evan Thompson’s work pair disciplined first-person reports with brain science, each constraining the other.

Phenomenology stands apart from the materialism-to-idealism debate. It sets aside the question of what consciousness is made of and describes what any answer has to explain. The main challenge concerns the reliability of first-person description. Jacques Derrida attacked the idea that experience is ever fully present to itself, and Daniel Dennett’s heterophenomenology treats people’s reports as data about what they believe, leaving open whether their experiences are as described.

Anomalous.summary: Psi phenomena, near-death experiences and altered states such as meditation and psychedelics may show that consciousness reaches beyond the brain. These are less theories of consciousness than evidence offered against reducing it to neural activity.
overview: This category gathers ideas driven by experiences that seem to break the usual rules. They include extrasensory perception such as telepathy and precognition, out-of-body and near-death experiences, reports of past lives, and the altered states produced by meditation and psychedelics. If even a small share of these turned out to be genuine and to defy physics as currently understood, the claim that consciousness is nothing more than brain activity would be in trouble.

Psychical research began in the late nineteenth century, and William James and C. D. Broad took it seriously. James proposed that the brain works as a filter, letting through a narrow slice of a wider consciousness, an idea Aldous Huxley later called ‘Mind at Large’. Dean Radin and Charles Tart ran laboratory studies of psi, and the Division of Perceptual Studies at the University of Virginia investigates near-death experiences and children who report memories of past lives.

The theories built on this evidence lean toward dualism or idealism but span every non-materialist position. Radin favors a quantum-oriented dualism, Tart an emergent interactionism, Carl Jung a collective unconscious linked by synchronicity, and Rupert Sheldrake morphic fields that carry memory through nature. Ken Wilber’s integral theory and Jean Gebser’s mutations of consciousness map stages through which consciousness develops.

Everything here rests on whether the evidence holds up. Etzel Cardeña’s 2018 review in American Psychologist argued that meta-analyses covering more than a thousand studies support psi. Arthur Reber and James Alcock replied in the same journal that psi effects are physically impossible and must come from flawed methods or chance. Replication problems and the dominance of anecdote over controlled study keep most scientists unconvinced.

Challenge.summary: Consciousness may resist explanation altogether. These views diagnose what is wrong with current theories, especially materialist ones, and question whether human minds can solve the mind-body problem, without offering a confident answer of their own.
overview: The Challenge category collects views that are better at diagnosis than cure. They argue that existing accounts of consciousness, materialist ones above all, fail in principle, and some doubt that any account will succeed. They mark the depth of the problem that every other category on the map claims to solve.

The best known is Colin McGinn’s mysterianism. McGinn argues that the link between brain and experience is real and natural yet may lie permanently beyond human understanding, in the way some concepts lie beyond the grasp of other species. Thomas Nagel, author of ‘What Is It Like to Be a Bat?’, argues in Mind and Cosmos that the materialist, neo-Darwinian picture of nature cannot account for consciousness and will have to be expanded.

Others attack the way the question is framed. Ludwig Wittgenstein and his follower Peter Hacker hold that much talk about consciousness misuses ordinary language. Raymond Tallis rejects what he calls neuromania, the habit of equating minds with brain scans. Eric Schwitzgebel argues that introspection is unreliable and that metaphysical humility is the right stance. Michael Shermer, David Eagleman and Sam Harris consider whether the problem may never be solved.

These views offer few positive proposals. Nagel goes furthest, suggesting that nature may contain a built-in tendency toward mind, while McGinn holds that the answer exists even though human minds cannot grasp it.
